Rare 1971 Plymouth Hemi Road Runner Flaunts Even Rarer Color Combo
8 photos
Photo: Geoff Stunkard's Zookeeper's Diary/YouTube
Unlike the Dodge Super Bee , which was discontinued after the 1971 model year, the Plymouth Road Runner remained in production for a few more years. However, 1971 was the end of the line for high-compression Road Runners, as Chrysler discontinued those engines altogether.
Mopar's decision put an end to the 440-cubic-inch (7.2-liter) Six-Barrel V8. The 390-horsepower powerplant had only been introduced in mid-1969. More importantly, the mighty 426-cubic-inch (7.0-liter) Hemi also went into the history books in 1971, after six model years on the options list.
1971 was the lowest production year for the 425-horsepower engine. Existing records suggest that only 355 vehicles were ordered with this mill in the US; the figure includes six nameplates. The Cuda is the most common, with 114 examples made, while the Super Bee is the rarest, with just 22 produced. The Road Runner you see here is one of only 55 units built.
The Mopar was recently showcased at the 2026 Muscle Car and Corvette Nationals (MCACN) , where it made its first public appearance after an extensive restoration. There's no info on whether it's a manual or automatic car, which keeps the actual production number under wraps. Of the 55 units made, 27 were fitted with the three-speed TorqueFlite automatic, while the remaining 28 examples got the four-speed manual.
But this car is rare regardless of the transmission, and I'd dare say ultra-rare when we factor in the color combo. The Road Runner is finished in Bahama Yellow, a somewhat brownish shade of yellow that was part of the Mopar high-impact color palette. Called Butterscotch on Dodge models, Bahama Yellow was only offered between 1969 and 1971.
The hue is rarer than the flashier high-impact colors, but it's the interior that sets this vehicle apart. The original owner went with a two-tone combo combining black and orange. The option was brand-new for 1971 and was discontinued for 1972. The combo is widely known as Halloween, though Plymouth did not use this name.
Historians label this interior as relatively uncommon. I've seen it in a few Mopars in recent years, but never combined with a Bahama Yellow exterior . The owner describes this Road Runner as a one-of-one. It may also have to do with a few other options (too bad we can't see the window sticker), but the color combo is probably the main culprit here.
The vehicle was restored by Apex Auto Restoration, and, needless to say, it looks flawless at first glance. It's probably one of the finest 1971 Hemi rigs out there, and I do hope we'll get a more detailed walkaround soon. Until that happens, you can see it making its first public appearance in restored condition by hitting the play button below.
By the way, these 1971 Road Runners can get pretty expensive when fitted with a 426 Hemi engine . They usually fetch over $150,000, but some examples can trade for significantly more than that. As of this writing, the most expensive units sold for $242,000 (2025) and a whopping $550,000 (2023).
